segments.text: Lightning never strikes the same place twice. Well, tell that to the Empire State Building. It gets hit about {20|twenty} times a year.
Lightning loves tall, pointy things. That's why the building has a rod on top, to give the bolt a safe path down to the ground.
Here's the wild part. A bolt is about five times hotter than the surface of the sun, but only about as wide as your thumb.
That heat makes the air explode outward. That's thunder. Count the seconds after the flash, divide by five, and you know how many miles away it is.
That's not all. A park ranger named Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning seven times, and survived every single one.
In fact, lightning flashes around {44|forty-four} times every second, somewhere on Earth.
So no, lightning doesn't avoid the same place twice. It actually prefers it.
